title: Ukraine’s child casualties reach highest level since 2022 as schools face repeated attacks
subtitle: UNICEF’s new figures record 114 children killed and 1,030 injured in the first ten months of 2026. Behind the toll are classrooms repeatedly repaired, interrupted lessons and families preparing for another winter of damaged services.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: A Kyiv kindergarten serving 60 young children was hit overnight on 7 November, after UNICEF had helped repair damage from an earlier attack. No children died at the kindergarten that night. Its pupils, aged about 18 months to six years, are now being cared for elsewhere, UNICEF said in a World Children’s Day briefing on 20 November.

The building’s second round of destruction gives a concrete meaning to figures the agency released the same day: at least 1,144 children were killed or injured in Ukraine between January and October 2026, the highest verified annual total since 2022, even with two months still uncounted.

The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine verified 114 deaths and 1,030 injuries. These are documented casualties, not an estimate of every child harmed by the war. They also leave out the much wider consequences of displacement, interrupted schooling and damaged public services.
A repaired classroom is not a guarantee of safety

Speaking from the damaged kindergarten, UNICEF’s acting communications chief in Ukraine, Louise Wateridge, described a facility whose windows, doors and classrooms had already needed rebuilding. A father told the agency that his five-year-old missed kindergarten and kept asking when he could return.

That account is a reminder that children want more than shelter from attack. They want familiar teachers, friends and a dependable day. Moving them to another building may preserve care, but it cannot by itself make that routine secure.

UNICEF said the United Nations had verified around 2,000 attacks on education since the full-scale invasion, including 270 this year. Those figures describe attacks on education; they should not be read as a count of distinct schools destroyed.

UNICEF says missiles and armed drones are putting families at risk far from the front line. Russia has repeatedly denied deliberately targeting civilians, Reuters reported on 20 November. That denial does not resolve responsibility for individual strikes, which requires investigation of the evidence in each case.
The school day that keeps stopping

The effects reach schools that have not been hit. In a separate assessment published on 3 November, UNICEF said air-raid alarms had affected 65.9 per cent of school days during September and October, compared with 37.4 per cent in the equivalent period of 2025.

Using data through 20 October, the agency calculated that alarms had overlapped with an average of 34 hours of scheduled learning. Alarm time is not a direct measure of learning lost: some teaching can continue in shelters, and conditions vary between schools. But it shows how often ordinary lessons must accommodate the threat of attack.

For parents and caregivers, the practical question is whether a school can keep children safe and maintain teaching when an alert sounds. Shelter access, continuity arrangements and communication with families matter alongside repairs to classrooms. A rebuilt school and a reliably functioning school are different achievements.
Winter services are part of child protection

UNICEF also warned of attacks on energy infrastructure as winter approaches. Its response includes alternative power for health facilities providing maternal and child care, support for heating and water systems, and winter cash assistance with Ukraine’s Ministry of Social Policy for more than 100,000 frontline households.

These measures protect the conditions in which children can recover, study and receive care. They also show why a casualty count, essential as it is, cannot capture the full burden on families. Electricity, warmth, water and dependable childcare are connected needs.

For donors and public authorities, the accountability test is therefore broader than how many facilities have been repaired. It includes whether services remain usable, whether displaced pupils can continue learning and whether families know where to turn when provision fails.

On World Children’s Day, the kindergarten’s story exposed the limits of asking children, parents and teachers to adapt indefinitely. Their efforts deserve support. The repeated destruction of the places they rebuild demands protection and accountability, not simply another repair bill.
